techniques.T1003: t1003 os credential dumping adversaries attempt to extract credentials from operating system caches, memory, or on-disk data structures such as the sam database, lsass process memory, or the active directory database (ntds.dit). credentials are typically recovered in hash or plaintext form and used for lateral movement, privilege escalation, or persistence via pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, or offline cracking. each sub-technique below targets a distinct extraction surface: process memory, an on-disk credential database, a registry secret store, or the flat credential files that mirror these same primitives on linux. lsass (local security authority subsystem service) a protected windows process (lsass.exe) that authenticates logons and holds the resulting credential material — ntlm hashes, kerberos tickets, and in older/misconfigured setups even reversible or plaintext secrets — in memory for the duration of a session. it is the single highest-value memory target on any windows host, which is why t1003.001 exists as its own sub-technique. credential material types ntlm hash (a fixed hash of the password, reusable directly via pass-the-hash without ever knowing the plaintext); kerberos ticket / tgt (a time-bound token that can be replayed via pass-the-ticket, or a krbtgt hash that can forge new tickets — a golden ticket); dcc2 / mscache v2 (a salted, iterated hash of a domain logon cached for offline use — cannot be pass-the-hash'd, only cracked offline); plaintext (recoverable only if wdigest or a similar legacy provider is enabled, or from an application that mishandles secrets in memory). sam vs ntds.dit the sam (security account manager) database holds *local* accounts for a single machine, at %systemroot%\system32\config\sam. ntds.dit is its domain-wide equivalent — the full active directory database, living only on domain controllers — and dumping it exposes every domain account at once, not just one host's local accounts. registry hive a hive is an on-disk file backing a section of the windows registry. sam, system, and security are each separate hive files; system holds the boot key needed to decrypt secrets in the other two, which is why adversaries almost always export all three together with reg save rather than just one. privilege levels required most of these sub-techniques need system or local-administrator rights on the target host (t1003.001–.005, .007, .008). dcsync (t1003.006) is different: it needs no code execution on a domain controller at all, only an account holding the replicating directory changes / replicating directory changes all ad permissions — normally domain admins, enterprise admins, and dc computer accounts. object access auditing (sacl) windows does not log handle or read access to files and registry keys (security 4656/4663) by default — it requires an explicit system access control list on the object plus the "audit object access" policy enabled. most of the file/registry-based detections in this guide only produce telemetry if this auditing was deliberately turned on beforehand; verify it's enabled before relying on those event ids in your own environment. volume shadow copy (vss) a windows service that creates a point-in-time snapshot of a volume. files that are normally locked while in use by the os — like an active ntds.dit — can be read freely from a shadow copy, which is why vssadmin create shadow shows up repeatedly in ntds and sam extraction procedures as a way around file locks. drs / drsuapi replication protocol the rpc interface domain controllers use to replicate directory data with each other. dcsync works by calling this same interface from a non-dc host and asking a real dc to "replicate" account data to it — the dc has no way to tell the request isn't coming from a legitimate peer dc, which is why the defense is access-control on who holds replication rights, not the protocol itself. /proc filesystem (linux) a pseudo-filesystem that exposes live kernel and process state as if it were files. /proc/<pid>/maps shows a process's memory layout; /proc/<pid>/mem is a direct read/write window into that same memory. root can read any process this way, making it the closest linux equivalent of dumping lsass. /etc/passwd vs /etc/shadow /etc/passwd is world-readable and holds account metadata only (no hashes since the shadow-password scheme replaced inline hashes decades ago). /etc/shadow holds the actual password hashes and is root-only (mode 0600) by default — the two files must be combined (e.g. with unshadow) before offline cracking tools can use them.
techniques.T1558: t1558 steal or forge kerberos tickets adversaries subvert kerberos authentication by stealing or forging tickets to enable pass the ticket. kerberos realms involve three parties — a client, a service, and a key distribution center (kdc) that issues the tickets after authentication. depending on which credential material an adversary already holds (the krbtgt hash, a service account's hash, or simply the ability to make requests as an authenticated user), they can forge a ticket that impersonates any account, forge one scoped to a single service, brute-force a legitimately-issued ticket offline, or lift a ticket straight out of a running session's credential cache. windows ships a built-in `klist` utility for listing and inspecting cached kerberos tickets. the three kerberos actors and two ticket types a client authenticates once to the kdc's authentication service (as) and receives a ticket granting ticket (tgt) — proof of domain authentication, encrypted with the krbtgt account's key. from then on, the client presents that tgt to the kdc's ticket granting service (tgs) to request a service ticket (tgs) for whatever specific resource it wants to reach, and that service ticket is encrypted with the target service account's own key, not krbtgt's. this tgt-vs-tgs split is exactly why golden tickets (which need krbtgt's hash) and silver tickets (which need one service account's hash) are forged differently and have very different blast radii. spn (service principal name) an spn is what binds a kerberos service ticket request to a specific service account — every service running under a domain account (sql server, iis app pool, etc.) registers one. by protocol design, any authenticated domain user can request a tgs ticket for any registered spn, no special privilege required. that's not a bug — it's how kerberos normally works — but it's also the entire precondition that makes kerberoasting possible: an attacker just has to ask, then try to crack what comes back. encryption types (etype): rc4 vs aes kerberos tickets are encrypted with one of several negotiable algorithms. rc4-hmac (etype 23 / 0x17) derives its key directly from the account's ntlm hash and is unsalted, which is exactly why an rc4-encrypted service ticket can be brute-forced offline straight back to a crackable hash. aes128/aes256 (etype 17/18) use a stronger, salted key derivation that resists this. a domain that has fully moved to aes-only kerberos meaningfully raises the cost of both kerberoasting and as-rep roasting — which is why 'unexpected rc4 in an aes-enforced environment' is one of the most reliable detection signals across this whole technique family. kerberos pre-authentication pre-authentication requires the client to encrypt a timestamp with its own key before the kdc will issue a tgt — proof the client actually knows the password, not just that it knows the username. it exists specifically to prevent an attacker from requesting as-rep data for an arbitrary username and cracking it offline. some accounts have it explicitly disabled (a legacy interoperability setting some applications historically needed), and that setting is the entire precondition for as-rep roasting. pass-the-ticket vs. pass-the-hash t1558 sits one layer up the credential-material stack from t1003: a stolen ntlm/dcc2 hash (t1003) still has to be exchanged for a ticket at some point to reach a kerberos-authenticated resource, whereas a stolen or forged ticket (t1558) skips that exchange entirely and can be replayed directly. that's also why several t1558 sub-techniques are direct payoffs of a t1003 dump — krbtgt's hash from t1003.003/t1003.006 becomes a golden ticket here. ticket lifetime as a forgery tell a standard active directory domain's default domain policy caps a tgt's lifetime at 10 hours ("maximum lifetime for user ticket"). forging tools default to far longer validity unless an operator deliberately overrides it — a multi-day or multi-year ticket lifetime on a 4769 event is one of the more reliable golden-ticket tells precisely because matching the legitimate default takes extra, easy-to-forget effort on the attacker's part. the pac: what actually carries the privilege, not just the identity a kerberos ticket doesn't just prove who you are — it carries a privilege attribute certificate (pac), an authorization-data structure listing the account's sids and group memberships, which is what a service actually checks to decide what you're allowed to do. the pac is signed by the kdc (with the krbtgt key, for a tgt), and that signature is the only thing stopping a client from simply claiming domain admin membership for itself. this is the real mechanism underneath both golden and silver ticket forgery: whoever holds the signing key can write whatever sids they want into the pac and sign it as valid.
techniques.T1059: t1059 command and scripting interpreter adversaries abuse the command and script interpreters built into nearly every platform to execute commands, scripts, and binaries. these aren't attacker tools — they're the os and its applications doing exactly what they were built to do, which is what makes this technique family so hard to blanket-block and so dependent on behavioral, contextual detection rather than simple allow/deny lists. the 13 sub-techniques below cover the major interpreters an adversary might reach for, from powershell and cmd.exe on windows through unix shells, python, javascript, and visual basic, out to network device clis, cloud apis, hypervisor shells, and container orchestration tooling. why this whole technique family is dual-use by design every interpreter covered here — powershell, bash, python, cmd.exe — is a legitimate, necessary part of the system it runs on. nothing about launching one is inherently malicious. that means detection here can't be about the binary's existence; it has to be about intent signals: what argued it, what it did next, whether the command line is obfuscated, whether the parent process makes sense. this is the single biggest mindset shift from a technique like t1003, where the mere presence of certain artifacts (a lsass dump file, a dcsync replication request from a non-dc) is itself a strong signal. living-off-the-land (lolbins) and why allowlisting alone fails most of these sub-techniques use binaries that are already present on the system by default — powershell.exe, cmd.exe, python (if installed), wscript.exe, osascript. an application-control policy that just blocks 'unknown' executables does nothing here, because nothing about these binaries is unknown or unsigned. this is why mitigations across this whole family lean on execution-prevention policies (constrained language mode, script signing, denylisting specific interpreters where they're not operationally needed) rather than generic allowlisting. in-memory script execution vs. file-based av a script interpreter can execute code that never touches disk as a file — piped in via `-command`, downloaded and `invoke-expression`'d directly, or run from a string in a scheduled task. traditional file-scanning antivirus has nothing to inspect in that case. this is exactly why windows added powershell module logging (event id 4103) and script block logging (event id 4104) to the powershell operational log — they capture what the interpreter actually executed, not just that it launched, closing the visibility gap file-based scanning leaves open. interpreter choice is about availability, not unique capability for an attacker, powershell, python, and a unix shell are largely interchangeable — pick whichever is already present and least likely to be flagged in that specific environment. a defense built around blocking one interpreter ("we disabled powershell") routinely gets sidestepped by simply switching to python, vbscript, or javascript instead, which is why several sub-techniques below exist as near-equivalents to each other rather than as a strict hierarchy of sophistication. encoding and obfuscation as the near-universal tell base64-encoded powershell (`-encodedcommand`/`-enc`), string concatenation to break up flagged keywords, char-code-built strings in javascript, obfuscated vba — this pattern repeats across nearly every interpreter covered here. it's one of the single highest-value generic signals in this whole technique family: legitimate administrative scripts are very rarely deliberately obfuscated, so a genuinely encoded or heavily obfuscated command line is disproportionately likely to be worth a look regardless of which interpreter carried it. amsi: the one defense that spans several of these sub-techniques at once the antimalware scan interface (amsi) lets antivirus/edr engines inspect script content after de-obfuscation but before execution — it's what actually reads the real command behind a base64-encoded powershell blob. its coverage is specific and worth knowing exactly: powershell (version 5+), windows script host (so both vbscript and jscript, covering t1059.005 and t1059.007), office vba and excel 4.0 macros, and dynamic .net assembly loads. it does not cover python or perl at all — which is a real, documented reason some intrusions deliberately reach for t1059.006 (python) specifically to route around amsi rather than fight through it. "amsi bypass" techniques (patching the amsi dll in memory, reflection tricks to disable the scan) are themselves one of the most common powershell-specific evasion patterns in real intrusions, precisely because amsi is otherwise so effective against this technique family.
techniques.T1078: t1078 valid accounts adversaries obtain and reuse legitimate credentials to gain access, and the technique spans four mitre tactics at once — initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, and defense evasion — because a valid login doesn't just get an attacker in, it also lets them stay, escalate, and blend into normal activity all with the same mechanism. this is the technique family everything t1003 and t1558 feed into: those packs are about obtaining credentials, this one is about what happens once an attacker actually uses them. the four sub-techniques below split by account tier — default, domain, local, and cloud — because each has a different blast radius and a different detection surface when compromised. why this is the highest-success-rate technique in the framework no exploit, no malware, no vulnerability required — just a username and password (or a token) that happens to be real. industry testing has repeatedly found valid accounts succeeding in the overwhelming majority of tested environments, and a large share of real intrusions rely on legitimate credentials rather than malware or exploits at all. that's the throughline for this whole pack: it's not that defenses fail to stop an attack, it's that from the system's point of view there's no attack to stop — just a login. the four account tiers and why blast radius differs a default account (factory-preset, often never rotated) is usually scoped to one device or appliance. a local account is scoped to one machine, but password reuse across many machines turns it into something much bigger. a domain account is scoped to the whole active directory domain by design. a cloud account can be scoped to an entire tenant, and if federated with on-premises ad, can bridge both worlds at once. the sub-technique split below exists because the right response to a compromise scales completely differently depending on which tier is involved. why 'valid' defeats signature-based detection entirely a stolen credential produces logon events that are byte-for-byte identical to a legitimate one — same protocol, same success code, same absence of any exploit artifact. there is no malware signature to catch and no anomalous process to flag. this is why every detection strategy across this pack is behavioral rather than signature-based: unusual timing, impossible geographic travel between two sign-ins, a service account suddenly used interactively, an account authenticating to far more hosts than its normal pattern. the whole discipline shifts from "is this bad" to "is this normal for this specific identity." mfa as the actual circuit-breaker, and why it isn't always one nearly every mitigation across all four sub-techniques below leads back to multi-factor authentication, because a password alone stops being sufficient the moment a second factor is required — which is exactly why credential-only theft (t1003, password spraying, phishing) increasingly isn't enough on its own anymore. but mfa isn't absolute: session/refresh tokens issued after a successful mfa challenge can themselves be stolen and reused for their remaining lifetime without ever re-proving the second factor, and mfa fatigue attacks (bombarding a user with push notifications until they approve one) target the human in the loop rather than the cryptography. both are why user training on push-notification hygiene shows up as a named mitigation here, not just technical controls.
techniques.T1021: t1021 remote services adversaries use valid accounts to authenticate to services that support remote connections — rdp, smb, ssh, vnc, winrm, dcom, and their cloud equivalents — and once inside, use the built-in legitimate remote-access functionality of the operating system or cloud platform itself to move from host to host. this is the direct payoff of t1078: valid accounts establish that a credential works, t1021 is what an attacker actually does with network reach and that credential in hand. the 8 sub-techniques below split by protocol, not by sophistication — which one gets used is almost always a question of what's already open on the target, not which is more advanced. protocol choice is availability, not skill level rdp, ssh, smb, winrm, vnc, and dcom are not a ladder of increasing attacker sophistication — they're six different doors, and an intruder picks whichever one is already unlocked on this specific target. a windows shop with rdp wide open gets rdp; a linux-heavy environment gets ssh; a host with no remote gui service at all but an open admin share gets smb. this mirrors the interpreter-interchangeability idea from t1059: defending against just one of these protocols leaves the other five completely untouched. interactive vs. non-interactive access — different capability, different telemetry rdp and vnc hand an attacker a full graphical session — they see what a user would see and can use any gui tool already installed. smb, winrm, dcom, and ssh give command execution without ever rendering a desktop. that split matters twice: it shapes what an attacker can accomplish immediately (gui tooling vs. command-line only), and it shapes what shows up in logs — a remoteinteractive logon behaves very differently from a scripted remote command, which is exactly why each sub-technique below has its own distinct detection fingerprint rather than one generic "remote logon" signal covering all of them. authentication proves identity; it rarely scopes what that identity can then do every protocol in this pack authenticates a connection — checks that the credential is real — but does comparatively little to restrict what an authenticated session can subsequently touch beyond coarse group membership (local admin, domain admins). that gap is exactly why network segmentation, rdp gateways, winrm trustedhosts scoping, and ssh allow-lists carry so much of the actual access-control weight in the mitigations below — the protocols themselves were largely never designed to do that job. cloud remote services: lateral movement without network adjacency t1021.007 and t1021.008 extend this exact same valid-account-plus-remote-access pattern into infrastructure that has no traditional network boundary at all. a federated cloud identity can reach a console or vm connect feature from anywhere on the internet — an attacker doesn't need to be on the same network segment, or any network segment the victim controls, to "move laterally" in the cloud sense. that's a meaningful shift from everything else in this pack, where physical or logical network reach was always a precondition.
techniques.T1055: t1055 process injection adversaries execute arbitrary code inside the address space of a separate, already-running process. the code inherits that host process's identity — its code-signing reputation, its network access rules, its position on any allow-list, and often its privileges — while masking execution under a name that looks completely legitimate to anything checking process names or file signatures. the 12 sub-techniques below split largely by platform and by which specific os mechanism gets abused to get code running inside someone else's process: windows thread/pe-loader apis for most of them, and linux's debugging (ptrace) or dynamic-linking (vdso/got) internals for the rest. why nearly every mitigation here is the same one look through the mitigations on each sub-technique below and you'll see m1040 (behavior prevention on endpoint) again and again, often as the only one listed. that's not an oversight — every api this pack abuses (virtualallocex, writeprocessmemory, createremotethread, ptrace, window messaging) exists for entirely legitimate reasons: debuggers, dll loaders, accessibility tools, automation frameworks. there's no "disable this feature" switch the way there is for winrm or vnc. the only real defense is behavioral — watching for the specific sequence of otherwise-ordinary calls that, together, only makes sense as injection. the point isn't what the code does — it's whose name it runs under a security tool asking "is explorer.exe malicious" will always answer no, correctly, because explorer.exe genuinely isn't the malicious file on disk. the entire value of every technique in this pack is that the resulting execution happens inside a process whose reputation, signature, and permissions were never actually compromised — only borrowed for the duration of the injected code's execution. the common three-step skeleton most windows sub-techniques share open a handle to the target (openprocess/openthread), get code into its memory (virtualallocex + writeprocessmemory, or an equivalent), then trigger execution. that last step is where most of the sub-techniques below actually differ: createremotethread is the textbook version, but queueuserapc, setthreadcontext+resumethread, a tls callback, or a window message can all substitute for it — usually specifically because createremotethread itself has become so well monitored that alternatives are worth the extra complexity. sysmon covers this family, but not by default sysmon event 8 (createremotethread) ships active in any standard sysmon deployment and is one of the highest-signal, lowest-volume events available — legitimate software essentially never calls this api. sysmon event 25 (processtampering, covering hollowing and herpaderping) is different: it is not enabled by default and has to be deliberately added to the sysmon configuration. a team assuming "we run sysmon so we're covered" may specifically be missing the one event type built for t1055.012 and t1055.013 below. why the linux-only sub-techniques don't share a detection story with the windows ones t1055.008 (ptrace), t1055.009 (/proc memory), and t1055.014 (vdso hijacking) abuse completely different os internals than the pe-loader and thread-api mechanics the windows sub-techniques rely on — the debugging interface and the elf dynamic-linking mechanism, respectively. the high-level goal (run code inside another process) is identical, but the actual mechanism, and therefore what to hunt for, has essentially nothing in common across the platform split.
techniques.T1053: t1053 scheduled task/job every major platform ships a way to run code on a schedule rather than once, and adversaries use exactly that legitimate capability to make execution survive a reboot, a logoff, or the original delivery vector being cleaned up entirely. mitre lists this technique under three tactics at once — execution, persistence, and privilege escalation — because a scheduled task doesn't just guarantee code runs again later, it can also run under a more privileged context than the account that scheduled it. the 5 sub-techniques below split by platform and scheduler: windows task scheduler and the legacy at utility, linux/macos/esxi cron, linux systemd timers, and kubernetes cronjobs for containerized environments. recurring execution is the actual value, not the delay a one-time delayed execution is barely more useful to an attacker than running immediately. what makes scheduling worth the effort is recurrence and reboot-survival: a task that fires every few minutes, or specifically at startup, keeps re-establishing a foothold even after the host is patched, the user logs off, or the original phishing payload is deleted from disk. every sub-technique in this pack is really being hunted for its persistence value, not its scheduling mechanics. the universal shape: a definition plus a trigger every scheduler covered here splits 'what to run' from 'when to run it' into two linked artifacts — a windows scheduled task's action and trigger, a crontab line's command and time fields, a systemd .service paired with a .timer, a kubernetes job template paired with a cronjob's schedule. that consistent shape is exactly why detection has to correlate both halves: a hunt that only watches for new task/unit/crontab creation without also checking what it actually runs will miss the part that tells you whether it's malicious. why this is a privilege-escalation vector, not just persistence several of these mechanisms let a task execute under a more privileged context than the user who scheduled it — a windows task set to run as system, a cron job dropped by a low-privilege web shell into a root-owned crontab, a kubernetes cronjob whose pod spec requests a privileged container. scheduling something is often the easy part; getting it to run as someone more powerful than you is the actual objective, which is why this technique sits under privilege escalation as much as persistence. hiding from the tool's own management interface, not just from logs windows task scheduler specifically can be made to hide a task from both the task scheduler gui and schtasks /query by deleting or corrupting its security descriptor registry value, while the task keeps running exactly as scheduled underneath. that means 'the task doesn't show up when i look' is not the same as 'the task doesn't exist' — a hunt has to check the underlying registry/filesystem artifacts directly rather than trusting each scheduler's own enumeration tooling.

subtechniques.T1003.001: t1003.001 lsass memory the local security authority subsystem service (lsass) holds credential material generated during user logon in process memory. with administrative or system-level access, an adversary can open a handle to lsass.exe and either harvest credentials in-memory or dump the process to disk for offline analysis with tools like mimikatz. common execution paths include mimikatz's sekurlsa module, sysinternals-style procdump, the built-in comsvcs.dll minidump export invoked through rundll32.exe, and abuse of windows error reporting (silent process exit) to trigger a crash dump of lsass on demand. why lsass holds credentials at all: the ssp architecture at startup lsass loads a set of security support provider (ssp) dlls — msv1_0.dll (ntlm), kerberos.dll (kerberos), wdigest.dll (wdigest), tspkg.dll/livessp.dll (terminal services/live sso) — and each one keeps its own copy of credential material in memory so the user isn't re-prompted for a password on every authentication (single sign-on). sekurlsa::logonpasswords in mimikatz simply walks each ssp's internal memory structures and prints what it finds; it isn't exploiting a bug, it's reading data lsass is deliberately keeping around for sso. why some dumps show a plaintext password wdigest, one of those ssps, historically kept a reversibly-encrypted copy of the plaintext password (needed to answer http digest auth challenges). since windows 8.1 / server 2012 r2, and via kb2871997 on backported older systems, the registry value hklm\system\currentcontrolset\control\securityproviders\wdigest\uselogoncredential defaults to 0, which stops wdigest from caching it. a lsass dump that yields plaintext almost always means this value was explicitly set back to 1, or the host predates the patch. the grantedaccess mask is the actual fingerprint to read another process's memory, a caller needs a handle to it obtained via openprocess() with specific access rights (process_vm_read, process_query_information, etc.), and windows encodes exactly which rights were granted as a bitmask. sysmon 10 logs that mask verbatim as grantedaccess — values like 0x1010 or 0x1fffff aren't arbitrary detection strings, they're the literal access rights a credential-reading tool needs, which is why they're such a reliable signal. why file-based and api-based dumping produce the same result mimikatz's in-memory reading and the comsvcs.dll/procdump file-dumping route both ultimately rely on the same os capability: a full memory snapshot of lsass.exe (via minidumpwritedump in dbghelp.dll, or equivalent direct memory reads). once a .dmp file exists, it can be moved off-box and parsed offline with mimikatz's minidump module with no live access to the original host required — this is why detecting the dump file's creation matters as much as detecting the initial process-access. how protected process light (ppl) actually stops this credential guard and ppl work by marking lsass.exe itself as a protected process in the kernel. once protected, even an administrator-token process's openprocess() call against it is rejected outright by the kernel unless the calling process is itself signed and running as a protected process of equal or higher level — this is a kernel-enforced access check, not something a normal admin tool (including most dumping utilities) can bypass, which is why m1025/m1043 are the mitigations that actually change the threat model rather than just adding detection. a non-security process opens lsass.exe with process_vm_read or process_all_access rights (sysmon 10 grantedaccess 0x1010, 0x1410, or 0x1fffff) and, within the same session, either writes a .dmp file to disk or loads comsvcs.dll via rundll32 -- the signature of a credential-dumping attempt against the account database of everyone who has authenticated on this host. lsass access is one of the highest-fidelity signals available on windows precisely because the legitimate-caller list is short and well-known (av engines, werfault, a handful of edr agents); once that list is excluded, remaining hits should be treated as near-certain rather than merely worth a look. sandworm team used the plainpwd mimikatz variant and rundll32.exe + comsvcs.dll to dump lsass. hafnium deployed procdump against exchange servers to harvest credentials post-compromise. volt typhoon targeted hashed credentials from lsass memory as part of a living-off-the-land intrusion set. cobalt strike injects into or reads lsass memory to extract password hashes via its built-in mimikatz integration. mimikatz sekurlsa::minidump and sekurlsa::logonpasswords modules parse lsass memory for plaintext credentials and hashes. sysmon 10 (processaccess) targetimage = lsass.exe with a grantedaccess mask indicative of full or memory-read rights (e.g. 0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1fffff, 0x143a). security 4656 / 4663 handle requested / object access attempt on lsass.exe — requires object-level sacl auditing enabled on the process, not on by default. sysmon 1 / security 4688 process creation for rundll32.exe with comsvcs.dll and minidump on the command line, procdump.exe, or task manager's dump-file helper. sysmon 11 (filecreate) .dmp / .mdmp file creation in non-standard paths shortly after a lsass handle event. lsass memory access (defender for endpoint) kql flags processes opening lsass with access rights consistent with credential dumping, excluding common legitimate callers. lsass dump via comsvcs.dll minidump sigma catches the built-in-binary lolbin path for dumping lsass: rundll32.exe invoking comsvcs.dll's undocumented minidump export. lsass dump via comsvcs.dll minidump (cortex xdr) xql cortex xdr equivalent of the comsvcs.dll minidump lolbin detection. mimikatz credential harvesting via sekurlsa sigma detects mimikatz sekurlsa/lsadump module usage by known command-line and originalfilename patterns. edr/av engines and windows error reporting (werfault.exe) legitimately open handles to lsass.exe with lower access rights during normal operation backup or system-state imaging tools that enumerate process handles across the system authorized troubleshooting by vendor support using procdump under a documented change ticket isolate the host if a lsass dump file was actually created, not just a handle-open attempt identify the accessing process: parent process, full command line, code-signing status, on-disk hash locate any created .dmp/.mdmp files and check whether they were staged for exfiltration (archive creation, outbound transfer) rotate credentials for accounts active in that logon session; escalate to a full domain credential reset only if compromise is confirmed to be domain-wide pivot on the tool's hash/behavior to hunt for the same activity across the rest of the estate m1040 behavior prevention on endpoint enable attack surface reduction rules that block credential-stealing from lsass. m1043 credential access protection enable credential guard (windows 10/server 2016+) to isolate lsa secrets; note hardware/firmware prerequisites. m1025 privileged process integrity enable protected process light (ppl) for lsa on windows 8.1/server 2012 r2 and newer. t1003.004 lsa secrets both surface ssp-managed or lsa-managed secrets from the same host; if lsass memory access is blocked by ppl, lsa secrets registry export is a common fallback path. t1558.003 kerberoasting a frequent follow-on once an attacker has working credentials: request service tickets for offline cracking rather than touching lsass again. t1550.002 pass the hash the direct next step once an ntlm hash is recovered from lsass — reusing it without ever cracking the plaintext.
subtechniques.T1003.002: t1003.002 security account manager the sam database holds local account credentials, normally enumerable only via apis like net user. with system-level access an adversary can extract it in-memory or export the underlying registry hives (hklm\sam, hklm\system) with reg save for offline parsing by tools such as creddump7. local rid 500 is the built-in administrator, rid 501 is guest, and rid 1000+ are regular local accounts — the values attackers are actually after. why system is required, and why reg save still works the sam hive's registry key acl restricts read access tds.dit on a domain controller, is the active directory database and holds credential material for every domain account. adversaries extract it via ntdsutil.exe's install from media (ifm) function, by creating a volume shadow copy of the dc's volume and lifting the file directly, or remotely via impacket's secretsdump.py over the drsuapi replication interface (which overlaps functionally with dcsync). it's an ese/jet database, not a proprietary format ntds.dit is built on the extensible storage engine (ese, also called jet blue) — the same database engine exchange uses for mailbox stores. that's why generic ese tooling like esentutl.exe can interact with it directly, and why offline parsers (impacket's ntds parsing, dsinternals) can walk the same well-documented table structure rather than reverse-engineering something bespoke. why volume shadow copy is the standard workaround like the sam hive, ntds.dit is held open exclusively by the ntds.exe/lsass.exe service the entire time the dc is running, so it can't simply be copied. vss solves this the way it solves it for any backup software: it creates a block-level, point-in-time snapshot of the whole volume, and files are read from that snapshot rather than the live, locked file — the copy operation never touches the actual in-use handle. two layers of encryption, same pattern as sam values inside ntds.dit are encrypted with a password encryption key (pek) that is itself stored in the database but wrapped by the boot key from the dc's own system registry hive. this mirrors the sam/system relationship exactly, which is why every real ntds extraction — ntdsutil ifm, secretsdump, manual vss copy — always grabs the system hive alongside ntds.dit; without it the database is just encrypted bytes. ifm is a legitimate feature being repurposed ntdsutil's "ifm" (install from media) mode is a real, microsoft-documented way to stand up a new domain controller without full network replication — it packages a consistent snapshot of ntds.dit plus the system hive specifically so a new dc can be seeded offline. the abuse in this sub-technique isn't a flaw in ifm; subtechniques.T1003.005: t1003.005 cached domain credentials windows caches the last several domain logons (dcc2 / mscache v2 hash format) at hkey_local_machine\security\cache, under subkeys nl$1 through nl$10, so users can still log on when a domain controller is unreachable. mimikatz's lsadump::cache module or the cachedump tool extract these; unlike ntlm hashes, dcc2 cannot be pass-the-hash'd directly and requires offline cracking. on linux, ad-integrated hosts running sssd or quest authentication services keep an equivalent cache at /var/lib/sss/db/cache.[domain].ldb or /var/opt/quest/vas/authcache/vas_auth.vdb. why the cache exists: offline logon a laptop that's off the corporate network — no domain controller reachable — still has to let a user log in with their normal domain password. windows solves this by caching a derived hash of each of the last several successful domain logons locally, and only consults it when no dc responds. how dcc2 is actually derived dcc2 isn't a simple hash of the password. windows first computes the standard nt hash (md4 of the utf-16le password) as an intermediate value (this intermediate is what's historically called dcc1), then runs that through pbkdf2 with hmac-sha1, using the lowercased username as the salt and 10,240 iterations, keeping the first 128 bits of the result as dcc2. the username-as-salt means the identical password produces a different hash for every account, and the 10,240-round pbkdf2 makes each guess roughly two to three orders of magnitude slower to test than a raw ntlm hash. why it can't be pass-the-hash'd pass-the-hash works against ntlm because a domain controller can verify an ntlm hash directly during authentication — the hash itself is the credential the protocol checks. dcc2 was deliberately designed the opposite way: it's a hash of a hash, salted and iterated, that windows compares only against another locally-recomputed hash during offline logon. a dc never validates a dcc2 value at all, so there's no protocol to replay it against — the only path forward for an attacker is cracking it back to the plaintext password. a process other than lsass.exe touches subtechniques.T1003.006: t1003.006 dcsync dcsync abuses the directory replication service (drs) remote protocol to make a non-domain-controller host impersonate a domain controller and request password data via legitimate ad replication apis — no code needs to run on a dc at all. any account holding the replicating directory changes and replicating directory changes all extended rights (normally only domain admins, enterprise admins, and dc computer accounts) can pull current and historical password hashes for any account, including krbtgt, enabling golden ticket forgery. mimikatz implements it in the lsadump::dcsync module. no exploit, no malware on a dc — it's a legitimate protocol call domain controllers stay in sync with each other by calling idl_drsgetncchanges over the ms-drsr protocol, asking a peer dc to send whatever directory changes it's missing. dcsync is simply an attacker's machine issuing that exact same call to a real dc. there's no vulnerability being exploited — the dc is doing precisely what replication is supposed to do; it just has no way to verify the caller is actually another dc rather than an attacker who happens to hold the right permission. why the permission is the entire security boundary since the protocol itself can't distinguish a legitimate dc from an attacker, the only thing standing between dcsync and total domain compromise is active directory's own access control: who holds the replicating directory changes and replicating directory changes all extended rights on the domain object. in a healthy environment that's dcs, enterprise/domain admins, and specific service accounts like entra connect — anyone else holding it (misconfiguration, over-delegation, or a compromised privileged account) can run dcsync at will. why krbtgt is the real prize dcsync can request password data for any account by name, but the krbtgt account is what makes it catastrophic: krbtgt's hash is the key used to sign every kerberos ticket granting ticket in the domain. once an attacker has it, they can forge a tgt for any user with any group membership offline — a golden ticket — without ever touching a dc again, which is why a confirmed unauthorized dcsync means treating the entire domain as compromised, not just the accounts actually queried. a 4662 audit event on a domain controller shows the ds-replication-get-changes or ds-replication-get-changes-all extended right requested by a security principal that is neither a dc computer account nor an entry on the organization's replication-rights allowlist (entra connect, approved ad-aware backup service accounts). this is one of the few hunts in this guide that should run as a standing detection rather than a periodic sweep subtechniques.T1003.007: t1003.007 proc filesystem linux's /proc pseudo-filesystem exposes kernel data structures per process, including /proc/<pid>/maps (memory region layout) and /proc/<pid>/mem (a direct window into that process's virtual address space). with root privileges an adversary can scan every running process's memory for credential-shaped strings; even an unprivileged user can inspect their own processes. mimipenguin and lazagne automate this against browsers, sshd, and other services that hold cleartext credentials in memory. why a filesystem path can read another process's ram /proc is a pseudo-filesystem — its files aren't on disk, the kernel generates their contents on demand from live process state. /proc/<pid>/mem is presented as a byte-addressable file whose offsets correspond directly to the target process's virtual address space; seeking to an address and reading is functionally identical to a ptrace(ptrace_peekdata) call, just exposed through ordinary file i/o (open/lseek/read) instead of a dedicated syscall. /proc/<pid>/maps is what tells a reader which address ranges are actually valid to read before attempting it. same permission model as ptrace, including yama hardening the kernel enforces the same access check for /proc/<pid>/mem that it would for ptrace: a process can only be read by its owner or by root. hardened distributions add the yama lsm's ptrace_scope sysctl, which by default further restricts even root/cap_sys_ptrace-capable processes from attaching to processes that aren't their direct children — meaning the practical detection surface is less "was /proc/mem read" and more "did a process with root or cap_sys_ptrace read the memory of an unrelated, sensitive process." what the scraping tools are actually pattern-matching mimipenguin and lazagne don't understand each target application's internal data structures the way mimikatz understands lsass's ssp layout — they take a cruder but effective approach: they know that subtechniques.T1003.008: t1003.008 /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow /etc/passwd holds user account metadata (uid, gid, home directory, shell) and is world-readable by design. /etc/shadow holds the actual password hashes and is root-only (mode 0600) by default. an adversary with root or sudo needs both files together — commonly combined with the unshadow utility — to feed offline crackers like john the ripper or hashcat, since the two files are interdependent for that purpose. why the hashes were split out of /etc/passwd in the first place early unix kept password hashes directly inline in /etc/passwd, which had to stay world-readable because ordinary tools (ls -l, id, getent passwd) need to resolve a uid to a username without root. the 1980s/90s "shadow password" scheme moved only the hash into a separate /etc/shadow file locked to root (mode 0600), specifically so any logged-in local user couldn't grab every hash on the box to crack offline — /etc/passwd was left world-readable by design because it no longer held anything secret. the hash string tells you exactly what you're up against the second field of each /etc/shadow line is formatted $id$salt$hash, where id names the algorithm — $6$ is sha-512crypt, $y$ is yescrypt (the modern linux default), $1$ is the long-deprecated md5crypt. that prefix is what tells an offline cracker which algorithm and cost factor to target, and it's also why modern distros using yescrypt or sha-512crypt with high cost factors are dramatically more cracking-resistant than older md5crypt hashes — unlike windows ntlm, these algorithms are deliberately slow by design. why unshadow is a required step, not optional /etc/shadow's hash field has no use without the account context in /etc/passwd, and /etc/passwd carries no hash at all — cracking tools like john the ripper want a single merged line per user (username:hash:uid:gid:...). the unshadow utility just joins the two files on username into that combined format;
